records.our_prose: Lettuce and carrots work as a classic interplant on root structure and timing. Lettuce is shallow-rooted and quick, carrots are deep-rooted and slow, so they pull from different parts of the soil profile and the lettuce canopy shades the surface, holding moisture and suppressing weeds while the carrots establish. Harvest the lettuce as the carrots fill in. This is a space-and-soil benefit rather than a pest one, and it is one of the more reliable interplants for that reason.

records.source_context: Soil health By planting plants with different root structures together, you can aerate the soil and allow plants to pull nutrients from different parts of the soil profile. Plants with taproots or tubers like carrots or potatoes can help to break up compaction in the soil.

records.our_prose: Carrots grow well in pots, which is great if your garden soil is hard clay. The main thing is a deep enough pot, deeper than the carrots will be long, and keeping the soil evenly moist. Choose a short or round variety for most pots, use loose potting mix, make sure the pot has drainage holes, and thin the little seedlings to about 2 to 3 inches apart once they are an inch or two tall.

records.our_prose: Dark brown to black, irregularly shaped spots with yellow halos appear first on the older, lower leaflet margins and tips; this is Alternaria dauci. Tan to gray circular spots with darker margins, showing on younger leaves and earlier in the season, point to the closely related Cercospora carotae. As the spots multiply they run together and the foliage takes on a scorched, blighted look, and large lesions can girdle and kill the petioles. The two fungi are difficult to tell apart and are managed identically. The roots are not infected directly but size up poorly when the canopy is badly damaged. A third, bacterial blight (Xanthomonas campestris pv. carotae), looks similar, with water-soaked, varnished lesions that track down the veins.

At later stages of disease development, dark brown to black irregularly shaped necrotic lesions develop on leaf blades and petioles. Leaves can be killed when foliar spots grow together or by lesions that develop on petioles.

records.our_prose: The diagnostic sign is galling: firm, beadlike knots on the feeder and lateral roots, distinct from the fine, soft secondary roots of aster yellows. The taproot forks, twists, and grows malformed, often with several prongs, because the nematodes enter the root tip and disrupt it. Aboveground, plants in affected patches are stunted and yellowish and pull from the soil easily. Galls from northern root-knot nematode (Meloidogyne hapla) are small; other Meloidogyne species make larger, more conspicuous galls.

records.our_prose: In peninsular Florida, carrots are a cool-season crop, so grow them in fall and winter and skip summer completely. Plant from about October through winter (you can start in September in the cooler north of the peninsula), and in the far south, stick to the middle of winter. Because the cool season is long, sow a short row every few weeks for a steady supply. Stop before spring heat arrives, because hot soil makes the roots tough and bitter. Carrots are usually ready about 60 to 75 days after planting.

records.our_prose: Northern-tier carrots run two sowings around a summer that is workable but marginal for root quality. Sow the spring crop as soon as the soil reaches about 40°F (UMN: late April to early May in most of the region, earlier toward zone 7, later in zone 3 where soils warm slowly); carrots tolerate cold soil and light frost. Sow the fall and storage crop in mid-summer, 10 to 12 weeks before the first frost (UMD), in the colder zones at the earlier edge. Carrots tolerate frost and can be held in the cooling ground or lifted and refrigerated for several months, so the fall crop extends well past first frost. Stop spring sowings before sustained heat, which turns near-mature roots coarse and strong-flavored. Days to maturity run about 60 to 75. Windows verified against UMN Extension, University of Maryland Extension, and MSU Extension; maturity against UGA Circular 1232.

records.our_prose: Carrots need deep, loose, friable soil free of stones, clods, and debris, ideally a light sandy loam or loam worked to at least 8 inches deep (deeper for long Imperator types). The texture matters more for carrots than for almost any other vegetable: roots grown in heavy clay or compacted ground grow poorly and come out forked, stunted, or misshapen. Work in well-rotted compost or manure before planting, but go easy on nitrogen, since excess nitrogen drives leafy top growth at the expense of root development and can cause forking and splitting. Moderate organic matter improves both moisture retention and friability; the goal is an open, stone-free root channel, not a rich heavy bed.

records.our_prose: Always direct-sow carrots into the garden; never start them in pots or cells. The taproot begins extending almost immediately and transplanting damages and misdirects its growth, producing forked or stunted roots. Direct-seed about 3 to 4 weeks before the last spring frost once the soil is workable and has reached at least 45°F, sowing seed shallowly (1/8 to 1/4 inch) and keeping the surface evenly moist, since a crusted seedbed blocks the small seedlings. Germination is slow, often 2 to 3 weeks; many growers sow a few fast radishes in the same row to mark it. There is no indoor-start or hardening-off step for carrots.

records.our_prose: For larger harvests, carrots are excellent long-term keepers. In cold climates they can be left in the ground under a thick straw mulch and pulled as needed until the soil freezes hard. Alternatively, pack unwashed roots in damp sand or sawdust in a box in a root cellar or unheated garage held near 32 to 40°F at high humidity, where they hold for months. Store roots only; trimmed tops are best used fresh or composted.

records.our_prose: Instead of planting all your carrots at once, sow a short row every 3 weeks or so. That way they are ready a few at a time over several weeks rather than all on the same day. In places with cool summers, start in spring and keep going into early summer, then sow one more batch in late summer for fall. In places with hot summers, grow them in fall, winter, and early spring and skip the summer heat. Carrots left in the ground too long in hot weather get tough and lose their sweet flavor, so stop sowing before the hottest part of the year.

records.our_prose: Even, consistent moisture is the rule, and it matters most in the first few weeks. From sowing until the seedlings are up, often 2 to 3 weeks, the surface must never dry out or crust, so light daily watering may be needed in warm or windy weather. Once established, carrots want steady moisture rather than a wet-dry swing: aim for about 1 inch of water per week including rain, delivered in deeper, less frequent soakings that draw the roots downward.
